headline: Earlier systematic review found high-quality evidence lacking for broad blue-light spectacle claims.
implication: Supports conservative claim language and defers to newer reviews for sleep-specific conclusions.
caveat: Pre-Cochrane review with overlapping but older literature.

headline: Public-health light consensus supports bright days, low evening light, and darkness during sleep.
implication: Frames glasses as one evening-light tool while preserving healthy daytime light exposure.
caveat: Does not test glasses directly.

headline: Simulated shift-work study found blue-blocking lenses prevented bright-light melatonin suppression.
implication: Supports the light-blocking mechanism while keeping shift-work questions separate.
caveat: Overnight shift-work physiology differs from ordinary pre-bed use.

headline: Orange blue-blocker lenses prevented bright-light melatonin suppression in an acute nighttime study.
implication: Mechanistically supports high-filtering amber/orange lenses rather than weak clear computer lenses.
caveat: Acute melatonin-suppression study, not a home sleep-outcome trial.

headline: Early small randomized trial found subjective sleep-quality improvement with amber lenses before bed.
implication: Supports a bounded evening test, especially for subjective sleep quality or winding-down signals.
caveat: Subjective outcomes, small sample, and baseline imbalance limit confidence.

headline: Ordinary evening room light can suppress melatonin onset and shorten melatonin duration.
implication: Room-light brightness is a major confounder; changing lighting mid-experiment can swamp the glasses signal.
caveat: Room-light exposure study rather than glasses intervention.

headline: Male-teen laboratory study showed blue-blocker glasses countered evening LED screen effects.
implication: Supports the screen-light mechanism but keeps pediatric/adolescent use separate from the adult protocol.
caveat: Adolescent lab sample; not a general adult home trial.

headline: Evening light-emitting eReader use delayed sleep and circadian physiology versus print.
implication: Track screen use, but do not add a new screen curfew during the glasses test.
caveat: Screen-light exposure study, not a glasses trial.

headline: Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder guideline frames timed light/darkness as clinical treatment, not generic sleep hygiene.
implication: Delayed-phase and other circadian-disorder protocols need separate clinician-guided pages.
caveat: Guideline context; not ordinary bedtime eyewear evidence.

headline: Small adult device-use crossover trial reported higher melatonin and better sleep latency/efficiency.
implication: Supports testing high-filtering glasses during the last two hours before bed when screens are part of the evening.
caveat: Very small sample and device-use context; room lighting and real-world adherence may change the signal.

headline: Inpatient mania RCT reported faster improvement with blue-blocking glasses as virtual darkness.
implication: Shows why mood-disorder protocols are separate and need clinician oversight.
caveat: Hospitalized bipolar mania with usual treatment; not home sleep optimization.

headline: Small delayed-sleep-phase study found evening amber glasses advanced sleep timing and actigraphic sleep onset.
implication: Relevant adjacent variant, but not direct proof for a general adult wellness test.
caveat: Open-label clinical circadian-disorder sample.

headline: Optical/clinical lens-performance study helps separate weak clear lenses from stronger filtering lenses.
implication: Product quality matters; require spectral or melanopic filtering data when possible.
caveat: Not a bedtime sleep intervention.

headline: Major-depression-with-sleep-onset-insomnia RCT is clinically relevant but not ordinary wellness evidence.
implication: Active mood symptoms should be outside the default self-experiment and clinician-guided.
caveat: Mood-disorder treatment context.

headline: Small insomnia-symptom crossover trial found sleep improvements with amber lenses for two hours before bed.
implication: Anchors the practical 90–120 minute pre-bed dose and makes subjective sleep onset a clean first signal.
caveat: Small, short insomnia-symptom sample with imperfect blinding; useful dose anchor, not definitive insomnia treatment evidence.

headline: AASM actigraphy guideline supports wearable sleep estimates as useful proxies, not ground truth.
implication: Pair wearable sleep-onset and sleep-efficiency trends with subjective logs before interpreting a personal signal.
caveat: Clinical actigraphy guidance, not a glasses intervention.

headline: Student crossover feasibility study shows adherence context but is too small for efficacy claims.
implication: Useful for burden and logging design, not for promising sleep improvement.
caveat: Young-adult student sample with feasibility framing.

headline: Recreational-athlete pilot found subjective sleep and morning-alertness improvements, but actigraphy did not significantly differ.
implication: Treat perceived sleep onset and pre-bed wiredness as useful signals while keeping wearable expectations modest.
caveat: Pilot sample and athlete context; not a broad adult efficacy proof.

headline: Translational metabolic/circadian study is useful hypothesis context but not a clean sleep-glasses trial.
implication: Do not add metabolic claims to the red-light-glasses sleep protocol.
caveat: Mouse plus clinical context with broader metabolic framing.

headline: Adjunctive insomnia RCT paired evening blue-light filtration with CBT-I, so glasses were not isolated.
implication: Relevant to insomnia treatment context, but not standalone proof for the consumer eyewear protocol.
caveat: CBT-I co-intervention prevents clean attribution to glasses.

headline: Actigraphy analysis of mania virtual-darkness treatment adds clinical sleep-parameter context.
implication: Useful for mood-disorder variant splitting, not independent ordinary-sleep evidence.
caveat: Secondary analysis from a clinician-guided bipolar mania trial.

headline: Smartphone study found spectacle strategies could reduce melatonin suppression, with lens properties mattering.
implication: Do not treat software filters, tinted lenses, and stronger coated lenses as interchangeable.
caveat: Mechanistic smartphone setting rather than ordinary sleep-outcome trial.

headline: Bipolar-disorder RCT tested adjunctive blue-blocking glasses for sleep and circadian rhythm outcomes.
implication: Do not generalize bipolar treatment protocols to an unsupervised sleep self-experiment.
caveat: Mood-disorder sample and adjunctive clinical care.

headline: Occupational experience-sampling experiments add real-world context but blend sleep, work outcomes, and chronotype.
implication: Do not make productivity claims on the bedtime sleep page; use it only as ecological context.
caveat: Work-outcome mediation is outside the protocol question.

headline: Double-masked RCT found blue-blocking lenses did not improve digital eye-strain symptoms versus clear lenses.
implication: Keep visual-comfort and headache claims out of the sleep experiment unless a separate eye-care page earns them.
caveat: Eye-strain sample, not bedtime sleep testing; no adverse events were reported.

headline: Healthy-adult randomized trial found no clear objective sleep improvement from evening blue-blocking glasses.
implication: Low-symptom users may see little or no wearable signal; the page should normalize null results.
caveat: Some subjective signals were modest, but sleep duration and sleep quality were not reliably better.

headline: Broad systematic review found promising signals across sleep and mood disorders but mixed populations and doses.
implication: Useful for landscape context, but it reinforces variant splitting instead of proving the default wellness protocol.
caveat: Combines insomnia, delayed phase, shift work, depression, and mania evidence.

headline: Pregnancy trial found full blue-blockers shifted melatonin profile earlier versus partial blockers.
implication: Supports circadian effect plausibility but not general adult sleep improvement.
caveat: Third-trimester pregnancy is a special population.

headline: Related pregnancy sleep RCT did not significantly improve primary sleep outcomes versus partial blockers.
implication: Keeps pregnancy separate and prevents using melatonin shifts as guaranteed sleep improvement.
caveat: Control lenses also blocked some blue light, complicating interpretation.

headline: Bipolar blue-light-blocking treatment review is mainly a safety and clinical-variant boundary source.
implication: Keeps bipolar or mania use clinician-guided and separate.
caveat: Research/practice review, not ordinary bedtime-glasses evidence.

headline: Indoor-light recommendations provide modern melanopic dose anchors but are not outdoor-efficacy evidence.
implication: Use the daytime minimum and evening/nighttime limits as implementation context for dose and timing language.
caveat: Recommendations target indoor environments and healthy adults 18-55, not all populations or outdoor protocols.

headline: Consensus guidance supports bright daytime light, lower evening light, and darkness during sleep.
implication: Supports evening-only use and prevents all-day blue-light avoidance framing.
caveat: Consensus light-dose guidance, not a glasses trial.

headline: Young-adult blue-light review shows daytime alerting benefits as well as possible evening sleep tradeoffs.
implication: Supports the evening-only framing and guards against treating blue light as universally bad.
caveat: Broad blue-light exposure review, not specific to pre-bed glasses.

headline: Melanopic irradiance predicted evening display-light effects on sleep latency, melatonin, and alertness.
implication: Use melanopic dose and screen/room brightness as implementation concepts, not just visible color.
caveat: Display-light mechanism study, not eyewear efficacy evidence.

headline: Systematic review/meta-analysis found possible sleep benefit from reducing short-wavelength light, but evidence was heterogeneous.
implication: Supports the broader evening-light-reduction idea without merging glasses, filters, and room-light changes into one causal claim.
caveat: Interventions and populations vary; use as landscape context rather than a direct product claim.

headline: Cochrane review found very uncertain sleep evidence and little support for broad spectacle-lens claims.
implication: Keeps the bedtime protocol from becoming an eye-strain, retinal-protection, or universal sleep-improvement claim.
caveat: Broader spectacle-lens review, not only high-filtering pre-bed amber/red glasses.

headline: Large psychiatric-ward blue-depleted evening-light RCT is a clinical lighting-environment variant, not consumer eyewear.
implication: Supports broader evening-light concepts while preventing ward-lighting evidence from becoming glasses proof.
caveat: Inpatient environment-level intervention.

headline: Commercial blue-blocking glasses vary widely; color alone does not prove melanopic filtering strength.
implication: Prefer spectral data when available, and keep fit, edge leakage, timing, and room/screen brightness in the protocol.
caveat: Implementation and product-characterization review, not a sleep-outcome trial.

headline: Schoolchild partial-blue-blocker trial advanced sleep phase and improved behavior without changing melatonin.
implication: Use as pediatric variant context, not adult wellness proof.
caveat: Children with myopia; pediatric use requires separate safety and outcome framing.

headline: Adult actigraphy meta-analysis found no statistically significant pooled improvement in objective sleep outcomes.
implication: Strongest direct reason to present the protocol as a personal test, not a likely wearable win.
caveat: Only three small crossover trials and 49 participants; null pooled estimates do not rule out subjective benefit for some users.

headline: Newer inpatient mania RCT did not significantly improve mania scores versus control lenses.
implication: Reinforces that psychiatric virtual-darkness evidence is mixed and should not be folded into the wellness page.
caveat: Clinical inpatient mania protocol and control-lens issues differ from consumer bedtime use.

headline: Home-lighting modeling shows lamp spectrum and brightness can change estimated melatonin suppression.
implication: Log room-light brightness and treat lighting redesign as a separate intervention from eyewear.
caveat: Modeling study; not direct home-glasses efficacy evidence.
